prompt.context: A friend at MIT has received a $20 million grant to develop a cool yet socially responsible technology. He has created a GPS device that is placed into a car and senses the type and severity of a car accident. It immediately transmits this information to emergency services, which then deploys resources to the accident scene. This service is most valuable for the more severe accidents, otherwise known as 'Type A' accidents. He is now considering a pilot in the Chicago area and wants your help before moving forward.
prompt.question: Question 1: How large is this market opportunity? Question 2: What methods should he use to price the device? (qualitative rather than quantitative answer)

clarifying_info.q: How many cars are in the Chicago area?
What percentage of cars get into Type A accidents?
clarifying_info.a: 1% of cars get into Type A accidents per year

clarifying_info.q: What is the average medical claim for a Type A accident?
clarifying_info.a: The average Type A accident medical claim is $100,000

clarifying_info.q: How much does the device save per claim?
clarifying_info.a: The new device should save $50,000 per claim

clarifying_info.q: What does the device cost to make?
clarifying_info.a: The fully-loaded device costs $400 (this is cost of making the device, not the price)

clarifying_info.q: What should we focus on for market sizing?
clarifying_info.a: Focus on medical claims only and the Chicago market. Focus on Type A accidents for simplicity.

framework: Market sizing (bottom-up: cars x accident rate x savings per claim)

questions.prompt: Question 1: How large is the market opportunity in Chicago for this GPS device?
questions.guidance: A good answer calculates the $500M number. A better answer uses a structured framework to arrive at it. A superior answer also discusses: new product diffusion curve (adoption over time), other values beyond claims savings (e.g., faster response, lives saved), and device compatibility across car types. Avoid getting stuck on the definition of 'market opportunity' — it is the potential value if product reached 100% market saturation and extracted 100% of the value, NOT (units sold x price).

math.setup: Market Opportunity = Device Savings Per Claim x Type A Accidents Per Year
steps: Type A Accidents Per Year = 1,000,000 cars x 1% = 10,000 accidents

questions.prompt: Question 2: How would you price this GPS device? (qualitative)
questions.guidance: A good answer covers multiple aspects of a pricing framework. A better/superior answer delves into specifics: Who is the customer (end user vs. insurance company vs. OEM)? Are there multiple customer segments? What environmental factors apply (defensible patent, government mandates)? Key elements: 1) Prepare marketing analysis (customer segments, targeting, positioning; competitors/substitutes). 2) Make marketing mix decisions. 3) Estimate demand curve. 4) Calculate cost. 5) Understand environmental factors. 6) Set pricing objective (profit maximization, revenue maximization, profit margin maximization, quality leadership, partial cost recovery, survival). 7) Select pricing method (cost-plus, target return, value-based, psychological, competitor-based, marginal pricing).

brainstorming.prompt: Who are the stakeholders interested in this GPS device, and what is their potential impact?

categories.name: Direct users
ideas: Family members of driver — emotional/safety interest

categories.name: Commercial partners
ideas: OEM manufacturers (e.g., Ford) — could install in new cars
Mechanics — could install in used cars
Investors — need for return on the $20M grant

categories.name: Institutional players
ideas: Insurance companies (health, life, P&C) — benefit from reduced claims
Medical community and emergency services — faster response times

categories.name: Broader stakeholders
ideas: Other party in accident — benefits from faster response
Competitors — risk of imitation; is the patent defensible?

recommendation: The Chicago market opportunity is approximately $500 million based on 10,000 Type A accidents per year and $50,000 savings per claim

Pricing should be value-based, anchored to the $50,000 savings per claim, but must account for the multi-stakeholder environment — insurance companies may be the true paying customer rather than the end driver
risks: Patent defensibility: competitors could imitate the device, eroding pricing power
Government mandate risk: if mandated, pricing flexibility is constrained
Adoption curve: 100% market penetration is unlikely in near term, so actual market capture will be a fraction of $500M
next_steps: Conduct customer discovery to identify the primary paying customer (driver vs. insurer vs. OEM)
Model adoption curve to project realistic revenue ramp
Engage Chicago-area insurers to explore value-sharing pricing arrangements
